source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: RCT
finding: Randomized trial of teaching founders to state theories and test hypotheses versus general startup training. Same hours of training in both arms.
numbers: 116 Italian startups, 16 time periods, 4-month training, stratified randomization; both arms got 10 sessions on market feedback.
limits: Mostly internet startups, mostly pre-revenue, Italy only; mentors and interviewer saw arms (not blind); small N.
agent_relevance: The effect is from a trained habit of theory plus test, not from more advice. A scaffold can imitate the habit.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: RCT (pivot)
finding: Treated startups pivoted more. 19 treated and 11 control firms pivoted at least once; 7 treated firms pivoted more than once versus 1 control firm.
numbers: 30 firms pivot, 41 pivots total. Linear coefficient 0.261 (p<0.05) on pivot count; negative binomial 0.803 (p<0.01); panel 0.016 (p<0.05). N=116.
limits: Pivot count mixes good and bad pivots; the later replication found the opposite sign (see b06).
agent_relevance: Testing assumptions should make the agent willing to change course when a test fails, not only to confirm.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: RCT (exit)
finding: Treated firms did not drop out more than controls on survival or time-to-exit. Exit counts were close: 24 treated vs 20 control exits.
numbers: 44 exits of 116. Cross-section exit effect positive and significant; survival and panel positive but not significant. Survey of 81 firms: confidence to abandon a startup 4.4 (treated) vs 3.2 (control), p<0.01.
limits: Self-report survey, one question, 1 to 7 scale.
agent_relevance: Falsifying tests did not make founders quit early; they made the stop-or-go decision more selective.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: RCT (revenue)
finding: Treated firms earned more revenue, but only 17 of 116 firms earned any revenue (9 treated, 8 control).
numbers: Cross-section linear coefficient 10,799.5 euros (p=0.010); 99% winsorized 2,666.8 (p=0.008); sinh transform 0.396 (p=0.065). Panel linear 674.97 (p=0.127, not significant); panel winsorized 172.5 (p=0.037). R2 0.22 to 0.28.
limits: Revenue result rests on 17 firms and is not robust to every spec (panel linear not significant, sinh only p=0.065). Heavy tail.
agent_relevance: Treat the headline 'more revenue' with caution. The sturdier result is the change in decision pattern.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: RCT (mechanism: time to events)
finding: Pivoting helped more when combined with the treatment. Cox models: interaction Intervention x Pivot raised hazard of customer activation (0.577, p<0.05) and acquisition (0.415, p<0.1).
numbers: Time_to_acquisition interaction 0.415 (p=0.093); activation 0.577 (p=0.039); time_to_revenue interaction 0.881 (p=0.228, not significant). Treatment alone on time to first revenue 0.253 (p=0.020) when pivot terms dropped.
limits: Not all hazard effects significant; authors call it suggestive.
agent_relevance: Better test discipline makes a change of direction more productive, so tie any pivot to a stated failed hypothesis.

source: Camuffo, Gambardella, Messinese, Novelli, Paolucci, Spina (2024) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: large scale replication and extension (SMJ 45(6))
finding: Large replication confirms the original: the scientific approach can be taught and gives better results. New twist: treated firms made FEWER pivots, and fewer pivots went with higher performance.
numbers: 759 firms in 4 randomized trials (working paper version; other listings give 754). Robust to instrumenting adoption with treatment assignment.
limits: Read from the CEPR abstract page only, not the full paper. Sign of the pivot effect differs from the 2020 study, so pivot count is not a stable outcome. Mechanisms named: methodic doubt (caution) and efficient search (better information).
agent_relevance: Success of assumption testing may show up as less thrash, not more. Judge the agent by outcome quality, not by number of plan changes.

source: Koning, Hasan, Chatterji (2022) Experimentation and start-up performance: evidence from A/B testing
finding: Cheap digital tests help high-tech startups, but naive comparison hugely overstates the gain because of selection. Adoption of A/B tools was staggered, and the true effect is about 10% more page views.
numbers: 35,262 startups, 2008-2013, 173 weeks. Only 7.6% used A/B tools at start, 16.75% adopted at some point. Raw gap 280% more page views; with firm fixed effects 46%; plus tech-stack control 11.8%; plus firm growth trends 8.5%. Event study: about 8% after one year, no pre-trend.
limits: Observational panel, not an RCT; web-visible outcome (page views) only; effect takes about a year.
agent_relevance: Expect selection traps when judging if testing 'works'. Any internal evaluation of the agent needs a control arm.

source: Koning, Hasan, Chatterji (2022) Experimentation and start-up performance: evidence from A/B testing (tail outcomes and product launches)
finding: A/B testing raised both failure and big wins, and more product launches. The authors read it as faster learning of what works and what does not.
numbers: Product launches up 9% to 18% (0.067 extra launches). Chance of zero page views up 0.7 percentage points; chance of reaching 100,000 page views up 1.4 points.
limits: Page views are a narrow proxy for performance.
agent_relevance: A good test makes dead ideas die faster. The agent should count a quick refutation as a success.

source: Koning, Hasan, Chatterji (2022) Experimentation and start-up performance: evidence from A/B testing (who benefits)
finding: Benefit depends on stage and experience. Older startups (about 5+ years) gain; the youngest (about 2 years) may do worse, though that interval includes zero. Experienced managers gain more.
numbers: Gain concentrated in firms founded more than about 5 years ago; 95% CI overlaps zero for the youngest; product-launch gain also mainly older firms.
limits: Moderator results are exploratory; interval overlaps zero for young firms.
agent_relevance: Testing before there is a stable idea can be wasted. Match test type to maturity: probe the problem first, optimise later.

source: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz, Koning (2023) The uneven impact of generative AI on entrepreneurial performance: field experiment in Kenya
finding: A GPT-4 business adviser on WhatsApp gave no average gain in revenue or profit. The effect split by baseline performance.
numbers: 640 Kenyan small business owners, half assigned to the AI adviser. Low baseline performers about 0.25 SD worse than high performers; low performers nearly 10% worse; high performers possibly over 15% better. Attrition 11 AI, 7 control.
limits: Heterogeneity is a subsample result. Press summaries said 8%; the paper text says nearly 10%. Advice was general, not an assumption-test protocol.
agent_relevance: Generic LLM advice does not make weaker decision makers better. The gain needs a structure that forces a test, not more advice.

source: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz, Koning (2023) The uneven impact of generative AI on entrepreneurial performance: field experiment in Kenya (mechanism)
finding: Difference was not in questions asked or advice given. It lay in which advice owners chose and put into practice. A model using question text alone predicted high vs low performer at only 43.2% and 51.8% in two checks (near chance).
numbers: Table 3 accuracy 43.2% and 51.8% (p=0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.61 in one check). Treated low performers were more likely to adopt generic advice; high performers used more specific words.
limits: Exploratory text analysis.
agent_relevance: Selecting which assumption to test is where value is made or lost. The agent should rank assumptions by risk and cost, not let the user pick the easy ones.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Eleven LLMs on a 2-4-6 style rule discovery game mostly test triples that fit their current guess. Higher share of falsifying tests goes with higher success.
numbers: 11 LLMs; task success 6% to 78% within 45 turns; reasoning-trace models show stronger success and lower bias. Metric I:C = incompatible to compatible tests. Positive correlation between I:C and success in both thinking and non-thinking models.
limits: Treats positive testing as bias; Klayman and Ha (1987) showed this can be a fine strategy when the rule is narrower than the guess. Synthetic number rules.
agent_relevance: A direct measured case for S7: an explicit step that forces a test which could prove the current assumption wrong.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models (prompt interventions)
finding: Human-derived prompts (Think-in-Opposites, Dual-Goal) raised discovery rates, from 42% to 56% on average. Think-in-Opposites improved success in all 11 model-inference settings, Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. Both raised I:C in 18 of 22 cases.
numbers: Average success 42% to 56%. Gains significant for thinking models (paired permutation, 50,000 permutations, BH-adjusted); mixed for non-thinking models (no significant I:C change; Dual-Goal slightly lowered accuracy). Example Qwen3-32B thinking I:C 0.14 baseline to 0.54 with TiO.
limits: 80 episodes per model-variant; open models mostly; non-thinking models did not move reliably.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt-level S7 step works for strong reasoners and may not for weak ones. Test on the target model.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models (distillation and transfer)
finding: Fine-tuning on intervention-guided traces cut confirmation bias and carried over to a new hypothesis task (Blicket test) and to math self-correction.
numbers: 8B model: AIME 2025 0.60 vs 0.33 (McNemar p=0.0386); Beyond AIME 0.40 vs 0.30 (p=0.0414). 32B: 0.80 vs 0.73 (p=0.6875) and 0.54 vs 0.52 (p=0.7539), not significant. Cross-scale distillation almost tripled Wason success and more than doubled I:C. GSM8K loss at most 2%.
limits: Small benchmarks, small N; gains only for the small model; our project does not train.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold-only agent the gain must come from a scaffold step, since weights are not changed.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models (human baseline, Wason 1960)
finding: Wason's original 2-4-6 study: more disconfirming tests went with correct first announcement.
numbers: 29 participants; 6 of 29 correct on first announcement; 21 of 29 eventually found the rule. Mean I:C 1.79 for first-try correct vs 0.24 for first-try wrong; 0.50 vs 0.19 on second announcement.
limits: Secondhand figures from the LLM paper's summary, not Wason's own paper. Small N.
agent_relevance: Gives the human reference level that LLM numbers are compared with.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: evaluating inductive reasoning in LLMs with rule discovery games
finding: Semantic version of Wason's task (WordNet categories) where the guess is narrower than the rule, so only negative tests can falsify. Reasoning models do much better, none near optimal.
numbers: 12 LLMs, 100 games each (1,200 total). Best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%; others 33-35%. Reasoning: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%. Small models weak: GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%.
limits: Task built so positive tests are useless; oracle (an LLM) errors exist (raw accuracy 85% to 95% versus human labels).
agent_relevance: Shows the effect holds outside number games and gives a size: strong reasoners about 70% vs about 35% for plain models.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: evaluating inductive reasoning in LLMs with rule discovery games (what drives success)
finding: Share of positive tests is the main driver of failure; oracle mistakes are not. Models that test more positively reach fewer conclusive falsifications.
numbers: Mixed-effects logistic regression, n=1,200 games: confirmation bias coefficient -4.15 (odds ratio 0.016); oracle error coefficient -0.12 (odds ratio 0.885, interval spans zero). Conclusive falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%; lowest Llama-4-Maverick 18.0% and GPT-5-Nano 26.6%.
limits: Hypothesis-target relation annotated by GPT-5-Mini; odds ratio is per full 0-to-1 change in the positive-test share.
agent_relevance: Track the falsification rate of the agent's own tests as a live metric in S7.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing (as cited in Jhaveri 2026 and Bertolazzi 2026)
finding: Rival account: a positive test strategy is not the same as confirmation bias. It can falsify when the guess is broader than the truth, and fails when the guess is narrower.
numbers: Described in the two LLM papers I opened; I did not read the original.
limits: Secondhand only.
agent_relevance: Pick the test by the relation of guess to truth: narrow guesses need tests outside the guess.

source: Chari and Pattanaik (2026) Wild guesses and mild guesses in active concept learning
finding: A rival view from a neuro-symbolic Bayesian learner with LLM-proposed programs. Information-gain queries beat positive-test queries when falsification is needed (compound or exception-laden rules), but lose on simple rules.
numbers: Number Game concept tasks; information-gain policy hurt on simple concepts through a support-mismatch trap (diagnostic boundary queries push the posterior to regions where the LLM proposes invalid or too specific programs). Positive-test policy converged faster on simple rules.
limits: Read the abstract and discussion only; no per-task accuracy extracted. Preprint, under review.
agent_relevance: Do not always attack the current assumption hard: use cheap confirming probes when the hypothesis space is simple, switch to falsifying tests when progress stalls.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of deontic conditional reasoning in LLMs: Wason's selection task
finding: On the Wason selection task, LLMs do better on deontic (permission) rules than descriptive rules, as humans do. Their error patterns fit matching bias better than confirmation bias.
numbers: Accuracy higher on deontic than descriptive rules for every model and prompt type, by 5.0 to 41.2 points. Fewer than 10% of humans solve the abstract version (as cited).
limits: Open models up to about 70B; selection task only; the paper notes it may not extend to other reasoning.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation: some confirmation-like failures are surface matching. Phrase assumptions so the negation of the claim is explicit.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to review its own answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels it looks good, but that is leakage.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1 self-correct) and 41.8 (round 2); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 and 74.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; HotpotQA GPT-3.5 26.0 to 25.0; GPT-4 49.0 to 43.0 by round 2. With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, GPT-4 97.5.
limits: Reasoning tasks only; prompt-based intrinsic self-correction only.
agent_relevance: A self-check is not a test. S7 must bring in new information (a tool, data, an outside reading), or the test is just the model agreeing with itself.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (answer flips)
finding: On GSM8K, GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time after self-correction. When it changed, it was likelier to turn a correct answer wrong than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 retained 74.7% on GSM8K; Llama-2 also often turned correct answers wrong on CommonSenseQA.
limits: Shown as figure; exact flip counts not extracted.
agent_relevance: Guard against the model dropping a right assumption just because it was told to doubt it.

source: Hirota et al. (2026) Aggregate vs personalized judges in business idea evaluation (PBIG-DATA)
finding: Experts disagree strongly on business ideas, so a single correct score is not available to check an LLM judge against.
numbers: 300 patent-grounded ideas, about 3,000 expert scores, six dimensions. Agreement on fine ordinal scores often near zero and sometimes negative; higher on coarse selection. Personalized judges beat aggregate judges on 5 of 6 dimensions in above-median Jaccard similarity (9-shot).
limits: Patent-derived product ideas, not real startups with outcomes; measures agreement, not truth.
agent_relevance: LLM idea scoring is weak ground truth. Use real tests against customers, not rated plausibility.

source: McGrath and MacMillan (1995) Discovery-driven planning (HBR); the subfield's source method
finding: Method: start from the required outcome, list every assumption behind it, and run checkpoints that test the riskiest first, as cheaply as possible. Spend follows evidence.
numbers: No outcome numbers from this source verified.
limits: Not opened. No controlled test of the method found in this session. The RCTs above test a related but different method (theory plus hypothesis tests).
agent_relevance: Design pattern for S7: reverse income statement, assumption list, ranked by cost of test and impact.

source: Kerr, Nanda, Rhodes-Kropf (2014) Entrepreneurship as experimentation (J Econ Perspectives)
finding: Economic theory: investors should fund many cheap experiments because outcomes are skewed and uncertainty is resolved by trying.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Theory piece, no controlled data from this source.
agent_relevance: Supports many small tests over one big bet when the test is cheap.

source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events (prospective hindsight)
finding: Imagining that an outcome has already happened is said to raise the number of reasons generated, often quoted as about 30%. Basis of the pre-mortem.
numbers: About 30% more reasons, quoted from memory.
limits: Not opened this session; number not verified. Lab study on written scenarios.
agent_relevance: Cheap way to surface hidden assumptions before testing: ask the model to write the failure story first.
